title: Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs)
description: Solve the XOR problem with hidden layers. Learn how stacking layers transforms feature spaces to solve non-linear problems.

slides.title: The XOR Catastrophe & Resurrection 💥
slides.content:
# The Limits of a Single Layer

In 1969, Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert published *Perceptrons*, demonstrating mathematically that a single-layer perceptron cannot compute the simple **XOR (exclusive OR)** gate:

* $(0, 0) \implies 0$
* $(0, 1) \implies 1$
* $(1, 0) \implies 1$
* $(1, 1) \implies 0$

No single linear hyperplane can separate $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$ from $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$. This historical finding caused funding for neural networks to evaporate for over a decade (the First AI Winter).

### The Solution: Hidden Layers!
By passing inputs through one or more intermediate **hidden layers** with non-linear activations, the network warps the feature representation into a new space where XOR is linearly separable!

slides.title: Single-Layer vs Multi-Layer Perceptrons ⚖️
slides.content:
# Architectural Comparison

| Dimension | Single-Layer Perceptron | Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hidden Layers** | None (Inputs wire directly to Output) | 1 to hundreds of intermediate hidden layers |
| **Decision Boundary** | Strictly flat linear hyperplane | Arbitrary non-linear curves, circles, complex manifolds |
| **Logic Capabilities** | AND, OR, NAND | Any Boolean function (including XOR, XNOR) |
| **Universal Approximation**| No | **Yes** (Universal Approximation Theorem) |
| **Training Algorithm** | Simple Perceptron rule | Gradient Descent via Backpropagation |

> 💡 **The Universal Approximation Theorem (Cybenko, 1989):**
> A feedforward neural network with just a single hidden layer containing a finite number of non-linear neurons can approximate any continuous function on compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ to arbitrary precision!

slides.content:
## Deep Networks vs Wide Networks
While the Universal Approximation Theorem guarantees that a *wide* 1-hidden-layer network can theoretically approximate any function, in practice *deep* networks (many narrow layers) learn hierarchical abstractions with exponentially fewer parameters than a single giant wide layer!
